_live_states_doc: The states and the District this site publishes: the one list of live states (2026-11-03g). build/status.py states() returns exactly this list; every public output (state pages, waters, the map's outfalls, the radar reads, coverage, the CSV downloads, the source tally) keeps to it, so water records and registry rows built nationally for other states sit in data/ without reaching the site. A state goes live by being added here, after docs/collection-checklist.md.

red.doc: Red covers reported ongoing discharges, post-discharge periods used by this site, and official advisories. The source and clock for each period are listed below. by_discharger entries (keyed by discharger id) take precedence over the state row.

MA.basis: Massachusetts requires notices to tell people to avoid contact for 48 hours after a discharge stops. This site counts those 48 hours from the reported end.

VT.basis: Vermont requires discharge signs to remain for 48 hours after an untreated discharge stops. This site uses that period for its status. Read Vermont DEC's notice for activity-specific advice.

CT.basis: Connecticut DEEP's July 7, 2026 guidance describes increased risk during rain and for 48–72 hours afterward on the Connecticut River and Long Island Sound. This site uses 48 hours after a reported discharge ends. That clock is a site interpretation, not the clock in DEEP's guidance.
CT.source: Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection (DEEP), guidance of July 7, 2026

RI.basis: Narragansett Bay Commission describes increased risks during rain and for up to 48 hours after a sewage discharge. This site uses 48 hours after the reported end. This is local guidance, not a statewide swimming rule.
RI.source: Narragansett Bay Commission, CSO Alarm Map

NH.basis: New Hampshire's law applies special water-use criteria during combined sewer discharges and for up to three days after they stop. This site uses 72 hours after the reported end.

ME.basis: The Maine sources reviewed here do not set a general post-discharge period. This site marks reported ongoing discharges and applies its own caution after they end. Official rainfall advisories follow separate rules.
ME.source: Maine Healthy Beaches program; Maine Department of Environmental Protection

NY.basis: New York's sewage notification rules do not supply a general post-discharge period in the sources reviewed here. Where New York City DEP gives an advisory end time, we use it.
NY.source: New York Sewage Pollution Right to Know Act; New York City Department of Environmental Protection (DEP)

NJ.basis: New Jersey sets no public notice period: CSO permits (Part IV.F.8) require outfall signs reading "Warning, possible sewage overflows during and following wet weather. Contact with water may also cause illness.", leaflets, a yearly mailing and a notification website; sanitary overflows and bypasses are reported to the DEP Hotline only (N.J.A.C. 7:14A-6.10)
NJ.source: N.J.A.C. 7:14A-6.10 and 7:14A-11.12; NJPDES CSO permit NJ0108812 (Camden City, 2024)

PA.basis: Pennsylvania sets no public notice period: operators report to DEP within 4 hours and in writing within 5 days (25 Pa. Code § 92a.41(b)) and notify known downstream users "if reasonably possible" (§ 91.33); CSO public notification is a permit control with no deadline; Erie alone falls under the federal Great Lakes rule (40 CFR 122.38: public notice within 4 hours)

MD.basis: Maryland sets no fixed public advisory period: a public advisory stays in effect until the local health department finds that sampling of the receiving water has returned to normal or prior background levels (COMAR 26.08.10.08D). Operators must report an overflow or plant bypass to MDE and the local health department within 24 hours and notify the public within 24 hours when it reaches shellfish, drinking-water, bathing-beach or recreation waters (Env. § 9-331.1; COMAR 26.08.10.03 and .08A). Local practice: Anne Arundel County closes affected waters for about a week after a sewage spill; MDE advises avoiding swimming within 48 hours of heavy rain
MD.source: Md. Code, Environment § 9-331.1; COMAR 26.08.10.03, .08A and .08D; Anne Arundel County Department of Health closings and advisories; MDE Healthy Beaches

VA.basis: Virginia law places no public notice duty on the discharger: an overflow must be reported to DEQ or the local emergency services office within 24 hours (Va. Code § 62.1-44.5 B; 9VAC25-31-190 L 6 and 7), and DEQ passes the report to the Department of Health, the media and its email and social lists only when VDH or DEQ finds a risk to health or water use, with no deadline (§ 62.1-44.19:6 B). Where an operator publishes its own post-overflow period it is applied under that operator's name

DC.basis: DC Water's permit requires a warning light on the Anacostia and on the Potomac: one colour while a combined sewer overflow is occurring and a second colour for 24 hours after it has stopped (NPDES permit DC0021199, Part III.B.1.h.i); DC Water's own page adds that after rain over one inch the effects can last up to three days. This site uses 24 hours from the end of the overflow, the permit's light period. No District law requires public notice of overflows, and swimming in the Potomac, the Anacostia and Rock Creek is prohibited by regulation (21 DCMR 1108.1)
DC.source: NPDES permit DC0021199 (EPA Region 3), Part III.B.1.h; DC Water combined sewer system page; 21 DCMR 1108.1

NC.basis: North Carolina law sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided. The operator of the sewer system or treatment plant must issue a press release to the news media covering the county within 24 hours of finding that 1,000 gallons or more of untreated wastewater reached surface waters, and publish a newspaper notice for 15,000 gallons or more (G.S. 143-215.1C(b)); every overflow reaching surface water must also be reported to the Division of Water Resources within 24 hours, and the Division posts these reports on its public map. On the coast, the Division of Marine Fisheries issues a swimming advisory and posts signs at swimming waters affected by a wastewater spill, with no set end (15A NCAC 18A .3404(b)). This site marks reported ongoing discharges and applies its own caution after they end
NC.source: N.C. Gen. Stat. 143-215.1C(b); NC DEQ Division of Water Resources, Information on Sewer System Overflows; 15A NCAC 18A .3403-.3404

GA.basis: Georgia sets no period after a spill during which the public is told to keep out of the water: the operator of a public sewer system must tell EPD immediately, report each spill of raw sewage to local television, radio and print media within 24 hours and to the local health department immediately, and post signs at the spill and at bridges, trails, boat ramps and other public access points downstream that stay up for at least seven days after the spill ends (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 391-3-6-.05(3)). A major spill (over 10,000 gallons) also needs a notice in the county's legal newspaper within seven days and notice to public water suppliers within 20 miles downstream. EPD's daily list gives the day a spill began, not its time or its end
GA.source: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 391-3-6-.05(3)(a)-(g); O.C.G.A. 12-5-30.1; Georgia EPD Sewage Spills Report

FL.basis: Florida sets no post-discharge period for the public: an operator must give the Department of Environmental Protection a notice within 24 hours of discovering a pollution release reportable to the State Watch Office, and the Department must post every notice on its website within 24 hours of receiving it and send it to county e-mail lists (section 403.077, Florida Statutes). Sewer overflows of 1,000 gallons or more go to the State Watch Office within 24 hours (F.A.C. 62-604.550). The Department of Health may issue beach health advisories when sampling fails its standards (section 514.023, Florida Statutes), and county health departments issue sewage-spill advisories at their discretion. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends

MI.basis: Michigan law sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided: whoever is responsible for a sewer system that discharges untreated or partially treated sewage must notify the Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE), the local health departments and a daily newspaper immediately and within 24 hours of the discharge's start, report its volume, receiving waters and times when it ends, and test the affected waters for E. coli (MCL 324.3112a). EGLE must promptly post each notification on its website, its MiEnviro list of sewage discharges, and combined sewer operators in the Great Lakes basin must give the public notice within 4 hours (40 CFR 122.38). Local health departments decide on beach advisories and closures from their own sampling. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
MI.source: MCL 324.3112a(1)-(3); 40 CFR 122.38; Great Lakes Water Authority CSO Public Notification Plan (2018); EGLE MiEnviro CSO/SSO List

WA.basis: Washington law sets no period after a sewage spill during which the water is to be avoided. The Department of Ecology must post on a public website each sewage spill reported to it under an individual water quality permit, with the estimated volume, the level of treatment, when it began, where, when it ended once known and the area potentially affected, and add the final information within a reasonable time after the spill ends (RCW 90.48.636); the law sets no posting deadline, and Ecology aims to post within five working days of the operator's report. Operators report spills to Ecology under their permits. King County and Seattle advise staying out of the water near a combined sewer outfall for 48 hours after it overflows; that window is used for the overflows their status map reports. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
WA.source: RCW 90.48.632 and 90.48.636 (2025 c 315); Washington State Department of Ecology, Sewage spills; King County CSO status map

CA.basis: California law sets no period after a sewage spill during which the water is to be avoided. Under the State Water Board's Statewide Sanitary Sewer Systems General Order (Order WQ 2022-0103-DWQ), a Category 1 spill is a spill of any volume that reaches surface water, or a storm drain that discharges to surface water without being recovered; Category 2 (1,000 gallons or more) and Category 3 (50 to 999 gallons) spills do not reach surface water. The operator must notify the California Office of Emergency Services within 2 hours of a spill of 1,000 gallons or more to waters of the State (Water Code 13271), file a draft report of each Category 1 or 2 spill in the Board's CIWQS database within 3 business days and a certified report, with the spill's end and receiving water, within 15 days of its end; the Board publishes these reports nightly. Category 3 spills are certified monthly, and spills from privately owned laterals are reported voluntarily. Whoever causes a discharge must notify the local health officer immediately (Health and Safety Code 5411.5); after a known untreated sewage release the county health officer must immediately post and close the affected beach until the source of the release is eliminated, and keep a telephone hotline of closed beaches (Health and Safety Code 115885, 17 CCR 7958). This site shows Category 1 spills, marks a reported spill while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; Category 2 and 3 spills are counted and not placed on a water
CA.source: Order WQ 2022-0103-DWQ 5.13.1 and Attachment E1 1.1, 3.1-3.3; Cal. Water Code 13271; Cal. Health and Safety Code 5411.5 and 115885; 17 CCR 7958

IL.basis: Illinois sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Illinois statute or rule requires the public to be told of a sanitary sewer overflow or a bypass: the permit's conditions require a report to Illinois EPA within 24 hours and a written report within 5 days, and these reports reach the public through the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's overflow records, usually days later. Combined sewer operators in the Lake Michigan basin, the City of Chicago, the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago and the suburbs of Cook County, must notify the public electronically within 4 hours of becoming aware of an overflow, post signs at outfalls and public access areas and tell the local health department (40 CFR 122.38); the District sends these notices by e-mail and text and shows possible overflows on a daily map. Other combined sewer operators notify the public under their permits. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
IL.source: 40 CFR 122.38; 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); NPDES permit public notification conditions (Nine Minimum Controls no. 8); MWRD permits IL0028053 and IL0028061, Special Condition 13.14; Illinois EPA sanitary sewer overflow form

AZ.basis: Arizona law sets no period after a sewage release during which the water is to be avoided, and no Arizona statute or rule requires the public to be told when one happens. A sewage collection system operator must report a release that is an imminent and substantial threat to public health or the environment (more than 2,000 gallons, or more than 50 gallons reaching a stream, a street, a public area or a building) to the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality within 24 hours and in writing within five business days; the only public duty is a warning sign, in a format the Department approves, at a location with more than three such releases in 12 months (A.A.C. R18-9-C305). The reports of plants with Arizona surface-water (AZPDES) permits reach the public through the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's overflow records, usually a few days later; systems that hold only an aquifer protection permit report to the Department, and their reports are not published. On tribal land, including the Navajo Nation, the permits are federal, the reports go to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the state rule does not apply. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; a report of a release that reached no water, or of a bypass held in the plant's own ponds, is not shown on this site
AZ.source: A.A.C. R18-9-C305(A), (F) and (G); 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); U.S. EPA sewer overflow and bypass event data (ECHO)

SD.basis: No South Dakota rule was found that sets a period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no South Dakota statute or rule was found that requires the public to be told of a sewage overflow or a bypass. Federal rules require every sewage permit to carry a report to the permitting authority within 24 hours and a written report within 5 days (40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); the South Dakota permit texts were not read): the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources, or the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency for the permits it writes in Indian country. These reports reach the public only through the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's overflow records, usually days later (a median of 5 days after the overflow began, in the records of April 2023 to November 2026). Under the federal policy for combined sewers, the permits of the two combined sewer operators, the City of Lead and the Lead-Deadwood Sanitary District, are expected to require public notice of overflows; no notice from either was found online. The Department posts harmful algal bloom advisories by lake, which stand until the end of the calendar year. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
SD.source: 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); 40 CFR part 127; NPDES permit public notification conditions (Nine Minimum Controls no. 8); South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources, Harmful Algal Blooms page

MS.basis: Mississippi sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Mississippi statute or rule requiring the public to be told of a sewer overflow or a bypass was found: operators report to the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality within 24 hours and file a written report within 5 days, since December 2025 through the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's electronic reporting system, and these reports reach the public through EPA's overflow records, usually days later (a median of 4 days from the start of an overflow in 2026). The Department issues water contact advisories for some rivers after large discharges as news releases, and posts beach advisories on its beach monitoring map and on signs at the beach. In Jackson, the overflow response plan of the 2013 consent decree calls for news releases and signs for significant overflows. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
MS.source: MDEQ, Reporting Sanitary Sewer Overflows or Bypasses in Mississippi (NeT-SewerOverflow); 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); 40 CFR part 127; MDEQ news releases of 2026-09-02 and 2026-09-08; United States and State of Mississippi v. City of Jackson (S.D. Miss.), 2013 consent decree

NE.basis: Nebraska sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Nebraska statute or rule requires the public to be told of a sewage overflow or a bypass: the permit's conditions require a report to the Department of Water, Energy, and Environment within 24 hours and in writing within 5 days, and the reports reach the public through the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's overflow records, a median of 23 days after the discharge began (2026-11-04 extract). Omaha, the state's one combined sewer operator, holds a permit that is expected to require public notification of overflows; its terms could not be read, and no web notice of Omaha's overflows was found. The Department of Water, Energy, and Environment and the Department of Health and Human Services put a lake on health alert when a weekly sample shows microcystin above 8 micrograms per litre; no advisory is issued for E. coli. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
NE.source: 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6)-(7); NPDES permit standard conditions and DWEE noncompliance form WAT098; DWEE publication 25-032 (NeT-SewerOverflow); NPDES permit NE0133680 public notification condition (Nine Minimum Controls no. 8, not read); DWEE Beach Watch

AK.basis: Alaska sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Alaska statute or rule requires the public to be told of a sewer overflow or a bypass: the operator of a wastewater system must report to the Department of Environmental Conservation within 24 hours when an overflow, a bypass or a spill threatens public health or water quality, and send a written report within seven days (18 AAC 72.940); wastewater permits add a written report within five days. The department does not post these reports. Reports that operators file electronically with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency reach the public through its overflow records, usually a day or more after the discharge began. Juneau's combined sewer permit requires that the public receive adequate notification of combined sewer overflows; the City and Borough lists its notices on its wastewater utility page. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
AK.source: 18 AAC 72.940; APDES permit standard conditions, Appendix A, Part 3.4; NPDES permit AK0023213, Part I.D.1.g; 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6)

NM.basis: New Mexico law sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no New Mexico statute or rule requires the public to be told when one happens. The person in charge of a facility must tell the New Mexico Environment Department orally within 24 hours of a discharge that may with reasonable probability injure health, animal or plant life, or property, in writing within a week, and report the corrective action within 15 days (20.6.2.1203 NMAC); the Department publishes no list of these notices. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency issues New Mexico's discharge permits, which require a report to the agency within 24 hours and in writing within five days; the agency publishes the reports filed electronically in its overflow records, and few New Mexico permittees file them. On tribal land, including the Navajo Nation, the permits are federal and the state rule does not apply. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; a report of a discharge that reached no water is not shown on this site
NM.source: 20.6.2.1203.A NMAC; 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); U.S. EPA sewer overflow and bypass event data (ECHO)

HI.basis: Hawaii sets no fixed period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided. For a spill into state waters, whoever owns or runs a wastewater system must notify the Department of Health immediately, send a press release to the news media for a spill of 1,000 gallons or more or one that threatens public health, post warning signs where the public has access, sample the affected waters until the Department says to stop, and report in writing within five working days (Hawaii Administrative Rules chapter 11-62, Appendix B); a spill onto the ground where the public has access brings the same press release and signs, with the report to the Department's Wastewater Branch; wastewater permits under chapter 11-55 add their own reporting conditions. The Department posts an advisory on its website and sends e-mail notices, and advises the public to remain out of the affected waters until it cancels the advisory. This site shows that advisory as the authority's own window, from the time the Department posts it until the time it cancels it. The Department's Brown Water Advisories, issued for storm-water runoff after heavy rain, are shown as rainfall advisories, not as sewage reports
HI.rationale: After the Department of Health cancels a sewage advisory, this site shows no caution period of its own: the advisory is the authority's own window for the water, the rule has the operator sample the affected waters until the Department says to stop and leaves the removal of the warning signs to the Department, and the site follows the authority's window in the same way for the Virginia Department of Health's advisories. A sewage advisory that leaves the Department's list without a cancellation is shown as end not confirmed
HI.source: HAR 11-62-06(g) and Appendix B (Responses for Wastewater Spills, Overflows, and Discharges, July 1, 2014), sections 2, 4 and 7 to 9; HAR 11-55; Hawaii Department of Health, Clean Water Branch, water quality advisories and events (eha-cloud.doh.hawaii.gov/cwb)

AL.basis: Alabama sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided. Its rule requires the permittee to report a sanitary sewer overflow that reaches a surface water or may endanger health to the Alabama Department of Environmental Management, the public, the county health department and affected water systems as soon as possible, and the Department's reporting form sets 24 hours with a written follow-up within 5 days; the rule sets no channel or content for the notice to the public, and petitions in 2017 and 2018 asking for one were not adopted. The Department posts every report on its public sewer overflow map within minutes of filing. On the coast, the Department of Public Health issues swim advisories from the beach monitoring program and lifts them when bacteria fall below the federal threshold. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
AL.source: Ala. Admin. Code r. 335-6-6-.12(l)6.(v) and r. 335-6-6-.02(hh); ADEM AEPACS SSO Event Reporting Form v1.5; petition to amend r. 335-6-6-.12 (Alabama Rivers Alliance and eight riverkeepers, March 2017); Coastal Alabama Beach Monitoring Program (ADEM and ADPH, BEACH Act)

TX.basis: Texas law sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and nothing requires a sewage spill to be posted on the web. Every sewer overflow must be reported to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality's regional office within 24 hours and in writing within five working days (30 TAC 305.125(9)); the Commission publishes these reports as open data in batches, months after they are made, with dates but no times and no locations. A local government's facility must also tell local officials and local media within 24 hours of a spill likely to affect a drinking-water source, of 50,000 gallons or more near one or in a sensitive area, or of 100,000 gallons or more (30 TAC 319.302). Texas Beach Watch recommends a beach advisory when a sample's enterococcus count is above 104 per 100 millilitres; local governments post it. Dates are read in Central time, and in Mountain time in El Paso and Hudspeth counties. This site marks a reported discharge from its start date to its end date and applies its own caution after it ends; a report is placed only on the water it names, and a report that names none is listed by its county
TX.source: 30 TAC 305.125(9); 30 TAC 319.301-319.303; TCEQ Sanitary Sewer Overflows (data.texas.gov 8kc5-95uk); Texas Beach Watch (Texas General Land Office); 49 CFR 71.9-71.10

UT.basis: Utah sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Utah statute or rule requires the public to be told when one happens. A sewer system must report a Class 1 sanitary sewer overflow (one that reaches waters of the state, exceeds 5,000 gallons, affects more than five private buildings or any public, commercial or industrial building, or may be a risk to public health) to the Division of Water Quality by telephone within 24 hours and in writing within five days, and smaller overflows only in its annual report; the Division publishes no list of these reports. The Department of Environmental Quality's public log of incidents phoned in to its spill hotline holds the overflows someone also called in, dated to the day they were discovered, with no end. Local health departments, with the Division, post advisories for harmful algal blooms and E. coli at monitored waters. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; a report the public phoned in is shown with this site's caution only
UT.source: Utah Admin. Code R317-801-4(4.1) and R317-801-1(13); Utah Department of Environmental Quality, Environmental Incidents (spill hotline log); Utah Division of Water Quality, Recreational Waters Map

OR.basis: Oregon law sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Oregon statute requires the public to be told of one. Every wastewater permit DEQ issues carries general conditions that require the permittee, when an overflow threatens public health, to alert the public, health agencies and other affected entities by its own Emergency Response and Public Notification Plan; no deadline and no channel are set. The permittee reports the overflow to the Oregon Emergency Response System by telephone within 24 hours and to DEQ in writing within five days, and neither report is published; DEQ's map layer of the spills it verified stops at March 27, 2025. The City of Portland publishes an advisory for each combined sewer overflow and for the sewage releases it reports, with the start and the stretch of water; its overflow advisories, and its releases to the Willamette, advise avoiding contact during the overflow and for 48 hours after it stops, and that window is used as the City's own where the advisory gives it. Times are read in Pacific time, and in Mountain time in Malheur County north of township 35 South. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; a report that says the sewage reached no water is listed but not placed on a water
OR.source: DEQ NPDES permit general conditions (Schedule F) and WPCF domestic general conditions; OAR 340-142-0040; City of Portland Environmental Services, CSO and sewage advisories; Oregon DEQ, spills reported to OERS and verified by DEQ, 2013 to March 2025; 49 CFR 71.9

KY.basis: Kentucky law sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Kentucky statute or rule requires the public to be told of a sewage overflow or a bypass. A permittee must tell the Division of Water immediately by telephone of a spill, bypass or overflow that may present an imminent or substantial danger to public health or the environment, and report it as the federal permit conditions require (401 KAR 5:065 Section 2(5)); the Division publishes no list of these reports. Kentucky's reporting system sent its reports to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's overflow records for December 2025 and January 2026 only. The Louisville and Jefferson County Metropolitan Sewer District posts its own overflow advisory on its website, asking people to avoid contact with the Ohio River, streams, drainage ditches and standing water "until 48 hours after the rain has stopped"; this site shows that advisory as the District's while the District's page carries it. Northern Kentucky's Sanitation District No. 1 alerts its subscribers from May to October when 0.25 inch of rain falls in its service area or the Ohio River rises above 38 feet, and keeps its advisories for 72 hours; this site applies the rainfall part of that rule at the District's combined sewer outfalls from radar rainfall. Times are read in Eastern time, and in Central time in the forty-one western counties. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; a report of a discharge that reached no water is not shown on this site
KY.source: 401 KAR 5:065 Section 2(5); 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); U.S. EPA sewer overflow and bypass event data (ECHO); Louisville MSD Overflow Advisory Level (louisvillemsd.org/overflowalert); SD1 Wet Weather Overflow Notification Program (sd1.org/218); 49 CFR 71.5(c)

TN.basis: Tennessee law sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Tennessee statute or rule requires the public to be told of a sewer overflow or a bypass. Sanitary sewer overflows are prohibited, and every permit requires the permittee to report any release that could threaten health or the environment to the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation within 24 hours and in writing within five days (Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 0400-40-05-.07(2)(n) and (o)). The Department publishes the filed reports in its Events Report, about five days after the event, with dates but no times, no receiving water and no coordinates; combined sewer overflows in Nashville, Chattanooga and Clarksville are permitted discharges and are not in it. The Department posts standing water-contact advisories on streams with high bacteria levels and issues harmful algal bloom advisories with their dates. Dates are read in Eastern time in the thirty counties of East Tennessee and in Central time elsewhere. A release is, by the Department's definition, sewage that did not reach water (0400-40-05-.02(75)). This site marks a reported discharge from its start date to its end date and applies its own caution after it ends, or for 72 hours from the start of its day when no end is given; a report is listed by its county and placed on no water. Each posted stream is shown as the Department's own advisory for as long as its list carries it
TN.source: Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 0400-40-05-.02(75), .07(2)(n)1 and (2)(o); TDEC Division of Water Resources Events Report; TDEC Bacteriological and Fishing Advisories; TDEC HAB Advisory Status; 49 CFR 71.5(d)

OH.basis: Ohio sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Ohio statute or rule requires the public to be told of a sewer overflow or a bypass: operators report them to Ohio EPA within 24 hours, and those reports are not published. Ohio's permit rule requires a permanent sign at every permitted outfall, combined sewer overflow and bypass outfalls included, and requires a major discharger near a drinking-water intake to notify the water supplier as soon as practicable. Combined sewer operators in the Lake Erie basin must notify the public within four hours of becoming aware of an overflow under their public notification plans (40 CFR 122.38); operators in the Ohio River basin notify under their permits. The Northeast Ohio Regional Sewer District, Akron, Columbus and Bowling Green publish their overflows; the Metropolitan Sewer District of Greater Cincinnati advises avoiding contact with streams for 72 hours after rain. Ohio EPA's spills layer lists the sewage spills called in to its emergency line, by day, with no end. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; a report with only a day is read in Eastern time
OH.source: OAC 3745-33-08(A)(12) and (F)(1); 40 CFR 122.38; 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); NEORSD CSO alerts map; City of Akron overflow status map; City of Columbus Sewer Overflow Discharge Information; City of Bowling Green CSO events; Ohio EPA Spills (Office of Emergency Response); MSD of Greater Cincinnati CSO notification program

MN.basis: Minnesota sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided. State law requires a discharge that may pollute the state's waters to be reported to the state immediately, and requires a publicly owned treatment plant and any public or private domestic sewer system then promptly to tell potentially affected downstream users, the public, Tribal governments and drinking-water facilities by the fastest means it has, and to post signs at affected public use areas or tell the body that runs them; the reports go to the state Duty Officer and are not published, and no statewide list of the notices exists. The Metropolitan Council posts a page for each spill from its regional sewers in the Twin Cities, with the warning signs it puts up and takes down, and the Western Lake Superior Sanitary District maps its releases around Duluth. This site treats the Council's warning signs as its own window, marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
MN.source: Minn. Stat. 115.061; Minnesota Pollution Control Agency guidance wq-wwprm1-43 and wq-wwprm1-59; Metropolitan Council, Wastewater Spills; Resource Renew (Western Lake Superior Sanitary District), overflow map

ND.basis: North Dakota sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no North Dakota statute or rule requires the public to be told of a sewage discharge. A spill or discharge likely to pollute water must be reported to the Department of Environmental Quality immediately, and the permits require an oral report within 24 hours and a written one within five days. Reports since 2021 go into the state's unified spill system, whose public list refuses automated reading; the Department's archive holds the reports of 1975 to 2020. The Department posts harmful algal bloom advisories and warnings by lake from May to December. Dates are read in Central time, and in Mountain time in the southwestern counties. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
ND.source: N.D. Admin. Code 33.1-16-02.1-11(4); NDPDES general permit NDG420000 Part IV(F); North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality, General Environmental Incidents - Historical and harmful algal bloom listing; 49 CFR 71.7(a)

MO.basis: Missouri sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Missouri statute or rule requiring the public to be told of a sewer overflow or a bypass was found: permitted wastewater facilities report them to the Department of Natural Resources within 24 hours of discovery, through its online portal, and those reports are not published. The Department's monthly concern reports, issued two to four months later, list the concerns it investigated; a concern is the reporting party's account unless the Department's comments say what it found. Kansas City's KC Water and St. Louis's Metropolitan Sewer District post some overflows on their own websites, and combined sewer operators post signs at their outfalls. State park swim beaches are posted 'Swimming is Not Recommended' when weekly E. coli samples exceed the state standard. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; a concern reported by the public is shown with this site's caution only
MO.source: Missouri Department of Natural Resources, sewer overflow reporting guidance (MoGEM) and Water Pollution Control concern reports; RSMo 640.080; KC Water news; MSD Project Clear alerts

KS.basis: Kansas sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Kansas statute or rule requiring the public to be told of a sewer overflow or a bypass was found: an emergency or accidental sewage discharge that a valid permit does not provide for is reported to the Kansas Department of Health and Environment immediately, and a planned bypass needs its approval seven days ahead; those reports are not published. KDHE issues a stream advisory, asking people to avoid contact with a stretch of water, when it judges one needed, and rescinds it by a later release; KDHE and the state parks agency post advisories for harmful algal blooms on lakes. The City of Leavenworth posts each of its sewer overflows. This site shows KDHE's advisories in KDHE's own window until KDHE rescinds them (14 days after the last read that confirmed one once its release has left KDHE's feed), marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; four western counties keep Mountain time
KS.source: K.A.R. 28-16-27; KDHE stream advisories (news flash) and Harmful Algal Blooms map; City of Leavenworth Sanitary Sewer Overflow Transparency Reports; 49 CFR 71.7(d)

AR.basis: Arkansas sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Arkansas statute or rule requires the public to be told of a sewer overflow or a bypass. Every permittee must report any sanitary sewer overflow, “no matter how small”, any unanticipated bypass, any upset and any unpermitted discharge to the Division of Environmental Quality within 24 hours, and in most cases in writing within five days, on the Division's online forms, whether or not it reached water. The Division publishes the filed reports in its Reported Noncompliance Incident Data search, current to the previous day, with the days the overflow started and stopped, the volume and whether the filer says it reached a stream, but no time of day, no coordinates and no receiving-water field. The Division posts harmful algal bloom advisories with the days they were posted and lifted, and the Department of Health lists the swim beaches it has closed, with no dates. Dates are read in Central time. This site marks a reported discharge from its start day to its stop day and applies its own caution after it ends, or for 72 hours from the start of its day when no stop day is given; a report is placed on a stream only when its location names one and the filer did not say it stayed on land
AR.source: Arkansas Division of Environmental Quality, Reported Noncompliance Incident Data (NPDES permit Part II reporting conditions as stated there); DEQ Harmful Algal Blooms advisories; Arkansas Department of Health, Arkansas Swim Beach Program; 49 CFR part 71 (Arkansas lies wholly in the Central zone)

WI.basis: Wisconsin law sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided. Every sanitary sewer overflow and treatment facility overflow must be publicly noticed promptly, by the communications the operator's emergency response plan names; the Department of Natural Resources' instructions make a notice to a daily newspaper the minimum when the overflow reaches surface water, and no web posting or hour deadline is set (s. NR 210.21(5), Wis. Adm. Code). The overflow is reported to the Department within 24 hours and on its form within five business days; the Department publishes none of these reports, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's tables held no Wisconsin report in their files of November 13, 2026. The two combined sewer permittees, the Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District and the City of Superior, are in the Great Lakes Basin and owe an electronic public notice within four hours of a combined sewer overflow (40 CFR 122.38). The Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District posts what it reported to the Department, with the dates and the volume, a few days after each overflow of its regional system. Times are read in Central time. Permits on tribal land are issued by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, and their reports go to it rather than to the Department. This site marks a reported discharge from its start to its end where the post gives both and applies its own caution after it ends; a report dated only to the day with no end shows caution for 72 hours from the start of that day, and one with a time but no end, or with only the storm's dates and none of its own, shows caution for 14 days from its report, then the end is marked not confirmed until 30 days after it began (after its report, when only the storm's dates are given); a combined sewer overflow that names no outfall is shown on every water the district's outfalls discharge to. Beach advisories and closures are the Department of Natural Resources' own, from its Wisconsin Beach Health system: each is shown at its beach from the Department's date of the advisory for as long as the Department lists it, and one for algae is shown as an algal bloom.
WI.source: Wis. Adm. Code NR 210.21(5) (as the DNR's form 3400-184 instructions give it); 40 CFR 122.38; Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District Storm Update posts; Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, Wisconsin Beach Health

DE.basis: Delaware sets no period after a sewage release during which the water is to be avoided. Anyone causing an environmental release, which for sewage means 10,000 gallons or more, must report it to the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control as soon as it is known; the Department must post it on its website no later than one business day after the report, and notify the district's legislators and registered neighbours within 12 hours of being informed. Discharges in compliance with a permit are exempt, so Wilmington's combined sewer overflows, the state's only ones, are not reported there: each outfall carries a sign. The Department's release list gives the release's time and place, not its end. The Department's Recreational Water Program posts advisories and closures at monitored beaches with their own start and end dates. This site marks a reported release while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
DE.source: 7 Del. C. 6002(20), 6014(b) and 6028(a); Delaware DNREC Environmental Release Notification System (Recent Releases); DNREC Recreational Water Program

SC.basis: South Carolina sets no period after a sewage spill during which the water is to be avoided. A wastewater utility must report a significant spill (5,000 gallons or more of untreated or partially treated sewage) to the Department of Environmental Services within 24 hours and in writing within five days, and give public notice within 24 hours of discovering it, through a channel the law does not name; the Department gives the notice when the utility does not. Spills caused by natural disasters, a third party's direct act or other acts of God are excluded. The Department publishes no list of the reports it receives. The City of Florence posts a notice for each overflow of 5,000 gallons or more. The Department posts swimming advisories at its beach monitoring stations and harmful algal bloom watches and advisories. This site marks a reported spill while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
SC.source: S.C. Code 48-1-95(A)(5), (B) and (E); City of Florence sanitary sewer overflow notices; SC DES Beach Monitoring; SC DES Harmful Algal Bloom Monitoring

IN.basis: Indiana law sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided. A combined sewer community must notify the affected public, local health departments, drinking water suppliers downstream and anyone who asks after its March newspaper notice whenever an overflow is occurring or imminent, in a manner agreed with each recipient, and post signs at public access points saying that sewage may be in the water during and for several days after rain or snowmelt (327 IAC 5-2.1); in the Lake Michigan and Lake Erie basins a public notice is due within four hours (327 IAC 5-2.2; 40 CFR 122.38). Sanitary sewer overflows and bypasses are reported to the Indiana Department of Environmental Management within 24 hours; the Department publishes no list of them. This site shows each combined sewer outlet's monthly totals from the operators' discharge monitoring reports with the monthly mark, marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends, and applies its rain caution at each open combined sewer outfall with a location once the outfall is placed on its water. Times are read in Eastern time, and in Central time in the twelve counties of the northwest and southwest. A report of a discharge that reached no water is not shown on this site
IN.source: 327 IAC 5-2.1-5 and 5-2.1-6; 327 IAC 5-2.2-1; 40 CFR 122.38; IDEM sewer bypass/overflow incident reporting (State Form 48373); U.S. EPA discharge monitoring reports and sewer overflow and bypass event data (ECHO); 49 CFR 71.5(b)

WV.basis: West Virginia law sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no West Virginia statute or rule requires the public to be told of a sewer overflow or a bypass. Whoever causes a spill or accidental discharge of sewage must report it by telephone to the Department of Environmental Protection's emergency spill line, and the permit's federal conditions add written reports; DEP publishes no list of these reports, and a 2025 bill that would have required public notice within 24 hours and an online spill database has stayed in committee since March 2025. West Virginia's combined sewer communities give notice by a sign at each outlet and a newspaper notice once a year; Charleston's sanitary board advises avoiding contact with the water around its outlets during overflow events and "for at least 24 hours thereafter", and Morgantown's utility board advised avoiding contact for 72 hours after rain (its page as read on November 9, 2026). Of the 61 permits with an open combined sewer outlet in the Department's outlet layer, none reported the number or length of its combined sewer overflows in the monthly reports the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency published for January 2025 to November 14, 2026 (as read on November 14, 2026); two report a monthly flow at one outlet, which this site shows as a monthly figure. This site applies its rain caution at each open combined sewer outfall with a location once the outfall is placed on its water (when radar shows 0.1 inch of rain in 24 hours there and no discharge is reported); an operator's own period is quoted as its own. Times are read in Eastern time
WV.source: 47CSR11 (Water Resources Special Rules; DEP emergency spill line); 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); EPA Combined Sewer Overflow Control Policy (59 FR 18688); WV DEP NPDES Outlets layer; U.S. EPA ECHO discharge monitoring reports; WV DEP algal bloom advisory map; Charleston Sanitary Board and Morgantown Utility Board combined sewer pages

LA.basis: Louisiana law sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Louisiana statute or rule requires the public to be told of a sewer overflow or a bypass. An unauthorized discharge is reported to the State Police hotline within the first hour when it is an emergency, or within 24 hours when it exceeds a reportable quantity, with a written report to the Department of Environmental Quality within seven days; the Department files the reports in its document system, whose search a CAPTCHA guards, and publishes no list. The City of Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge lists every discharge from its collection systems in its quarterly reports under a federal consent decree, with the day, the cause, the receiving water and the gallons, but no time and no end; this site gives each such report its caution for 72 hours from the start of its day, though the reports appear a month or more after the quarter, when that period has passed. Louisiana has no municipal combined sewer system. Times are read in Central time. A report that names no receiving water is listed but not placed on a water
LA.source: LAC 33:I.3915, 3917 and 3925; 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); LDEQ Single Point of Contact; City of Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge consent-decree quarterly reports (Part D)

NV.basis: Nevada sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Nevada statute or rule found requires the public to be told when one happens. Since 2025 a city, county, unincorporated town, general improvement district, wastewater district or water authority aware of a sewage discharge must notify the Nevada Division of Environmental Protection online or by telephone, with no deadline, and the Division notifies any Indian tribe that may be affected (NRS 445A.467); a discharge permit adds the permittee's report to the Division within 24 hours and in writing within five days. No published list of these reports was found, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's overflow records hold no Nevada report. Nevada State Parks post harmful algal bloom advisories (Watch, Warning or Danger) for waters in state parks, with the date of each update; the statewide bloom dashboard offered no data download when read on November 9, 2026, and the Office of State Epidemiology lists the state's active advisories, which this site does not yet read. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; a bloom advisory is shown while the parks list it, and no longer than 14 days after the last read that found it listed. Nevada's times are Pacific time, except West Wendover's, which are Mountain time
NV.source: NRS 445A.467; 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); 49 CFR 71.9(b); Nevada Division of State Parks, HAB Advisory; U.S. EPA sewer overflow and bypass event data (ECHO)

OK.basis: Oklahoma sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Oklahoma statute or rule requires the public to be told when one happens. The Department of Environmental Quality's standard conditions for municipal discharge permits require oral notice to the Department within 24 hours of becoming aware of any sewer overflow or bypass, and a written report within five days; the Department's reporting page asks instead for a telephone report within 48 hours of the event, and its bypass form for 24 hours, so its instructions differ. No published list of these reports was found, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's overflow records hold no Oklahoma report. The National Park Service posts its weekly E. coli results at the swimming places of Chickasaw National Recreation Area in summer and posts signs at the water when they are high. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; a park result at or above the park's threshold is shown with this site's caution for 72 hours from the sample, never as the park's notice. Oklahoma's times are Central time
OK.source: Oklahoma DEQ municipal OPDES permit Part III B.6 (March 2017); DEQ wastewater reporting requirements; DEQ Form 605-011 (October 2025); OAC 252:606; 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); National Park Service, Chickasaw National Recreation Area, Bathing Beach Monitoring Program

PR.basis: Puerto Rico sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Puerto Rico statute or rule requiring the public to be told of a sewer overflow or a bypass was found: the Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Sewer Authority (PRASA) and the other permittees report them to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, which writes Puerto Rico's permits, within 24 hours and in writing within five days, and EPA publishes the electronic reports in its overflow records with the day it received each (a median of 2 days after the start in 2025 and 2026), not the day each was published. PRASA's Puerto Nuevo permit requires a public notification process for its combined sewer overflows in San Juan, and its 2023 consent decree modification calls for posting them on PRASA's website; no posted overflow was found. The Department of Natural and Environmental Resources (DRNA) publishes a weekly notice of the beaches whose samples exceed the enterococci Beach Action Value, which it declares not fit for bathers; this site shows each as DRNA's own advisory from the notice that lists it until a notice says the beaches are fit for bathers; a later notice that only no longer lists a beach is not a lift: the advisory is shown until that notice, its end marked as first seen there, and for no more than 14 days after the last notice that listed it. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; times are read in Atlantic Standard Time, which Puerto Rico keeps all year
PR.source: 40 CFR 122.41(l)(6); 40 CFR part 127; U.S. EPA sewer overflow and bypass event data (ECHO); NPDES permit PR0021555 (2021), CSO permit conditions; United States v. PRASA, No. 3:15-cv-02283 (D.P.R.), 2023 modification; DRNA Programa de Monitoría de Playas y Notificación Pública (drna.pr.gov)

CO.basis: Colorado sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Colorado statute or rule found requires the public to be told when one happens. Whoever's activity results in a spill or discharge that may pollute state waters must notify the Water Quality Control Division as soon as they know of it, and the discharge permits require an oral report within 24 hours of noncompliance that may endanger health or the environment and a written report within five days; the Division publishes none of these reports, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's tables (of November 13, 2026, read on November 15, 2026) held no Colorado report. A large spill reaches the public when an agency issues an advisory, as Colorado Parks and Wildlife did after the Pueblo spill of August 2026; the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment keeps a public sheet of algal bloom conditions for selected waters. Permits on tribal land and for federal facilities are issued by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, and their reports go to it. Times are read in Mountain time. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
CO.source: C.R.S. 25-8-601(2); Colorado Discharge Permit System permit standard conditions (CO0032999, Part II); Colorado Parks and Wildlife news release of August 30, 2026; CDPHE toxic algae status sheet

MT.basis: Montana sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Montana statute, rule or permit found requires the public to be told when one happens. The discharge permits require serious noncompliance, a bypass or an upset to be reported to the Department of Environmental Quality or to Disaster and Emergency Services within 24 hours and in writing within five days, on the Department's sanitary sewer overflow form; the Department publishes none of these reports, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's tables (files of November 13, 2026) held no Montana report on November 15, 2026. The Department's harmful algal bloom map gives the date each bloom advisory was issued and lifted. Permits on tribal land are issued by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, and their reports go to it. Times are read in Mountain time. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
MT.source: MPDES permit standard conditions (MT0020168, Part II.I); Montana DEQ Sanitary Sewer Overflow Event Form (April 2020); Montana DEQ Harmful Algal Bloom map

WY.basis: Wyoming sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Wyoming statute, rule or permit found requires the public to be told when one happens. The Department of Environmental Quality asks whoever owns or runs a collection system or treatment works to report a sanitary sewer overflow to it verbally within 24 hours of becoming aware of it and in writing within five days; the Department publishes none of these reports, its spill system's search needs a login, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's tables of November 13, 2026 held no Wyoming report. The Department of Health and the Department of Environmental Quality publish bloom and toxin advisories with the date each was issued; an advisory holds until the bloom has dissipated or the toxins are below the recreational levels, or until December 31, whichever comes first. Permits on the Wind River Reservation are issued by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, and their reports go to it. Times are read in Mountain time. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends
WY.source: Wyoming DEQ, Sanitary Sewer Overflows (WYPDES program page, read 2026-11-14); Wyoming DEQ harmful cyanobacteria bloom program page and FAQ; Wyoming DEQ HCB bulletins (GovDelivery topic WYDEQ_42)

IA.basis: Iowa sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided. An unanticipated bypass or upset must be reported to the Department of Natural Resources field office by telephone within 24 hours and in writing within five days; the Department decides whether the public must be told, and then the operator prepares the notice. The field offices' records of the reports are public, one page per report, with the times, the receiving stream and the gallons the field office entered; this site reads them for the facilities the Department classes major municipal. The Department publishes a news release when it asks the public to stay away, and the City of Waterloo posts each overflow and bypass on its own page. This site marks a reported discharge while it runs and applies its own caution after it ends; a report that names no water is listed with its operator and county
IA.source: 567 IAC 63.6; Iowa DNR Field Office Compliance (incoming reports); Iowa DNR news releases; City of Waterloo, SSO & Bypass Public Notification

ID.basis: Idaho sets no period after a sewage discharge during which the water is to be avoided, and no Idaho statute or rule requires the public to be told of one; the federal permits read (EPA Region 10's 2026 draft for Kooskia and its earlier permit for West Boise) require the permittee to notify the public immediately by its own emergency response and public notification plan, with no channel or deadline set, and no such notice was found on the web. Permittees report overflows and other noncompliance to the Department of Environmental Quality (or, in Indian country, to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency) by telephone within 24 hours and in writing within five days; neither publishes the reports, so this site shows no Idaho sewage report. The Department of Health and Welfare issues cyanobacteria health advisories on the Department of Environmental Quality's toxin results; the Department of Environmental Quality's table also lists Health Watch and Health Alert risk levels while results are pending, which this site shows with its own caution, never as an advisory, unless the table says the water is closed to recreational use, which this site shows as the authority's closure. Dates are read in Mountain time, and in Pacific time north of the Salmon River
ID.source: IDAPA 58.01.25; the West Boise Water Renewal Facility's IPDES permit (modified 2024), sections 2.2.7-2.2.8; Idaho DEQ, CyanoHAB Risk Data Table; Idaho DHW, Recreational Water Health Advisories; 49 CFR 71.9; EPA Region 10 permits ID0023981 (2016 modification) and ID0021814 (2026 draft), Part III.I

pa-alcosan.basis: ALCOSAN's advisory log: "Overflows have ceased; Waterways may still be impaired." stands until 48 hours after overflows end (the Allegheny County Health Department cancels its alerts 24 to 36 hours after)
pa-alcosan.source: ALCOSAN sewer overflow advisories; Allegheny County Health Department FAQ

va-richmond-dpu.basis: Richmond's combined sewer overflow map marks each outfall red for 48 hours after an overflow (legend: "in the last 48 hours")
va-richmond-dpu.source: City of Richmond Department of Public Utilities CSO notification map

va-alexrenew.basis: AlexRenew's CSO status layer shows an outfall red when an overflow occurred in the past 24 hours
va-alexrenew.source: AlexRenew combined sewer overflow status map

va-lynchburg-water-resources.basis: Lynchburg sends a second CSO alert thirty hours after an overflow ends
va-lynchburg-water-resources.source: Lynchburg Alerts (Department of Water Resources CSO notifications)

yellow.doc: DirtyWaterWatch sets these caution periods using the studies listed below. Periods count from the reported discharge end, not from the end of the red period.
yellow.default_rationale: We use 72 hours after the reported discharge end as our standard caution period. The cited studies describe bacteria or illness after rain and sewage exposure in other settings. They do not establish when a particular New England water becomes safe. Local conditions can extend contamination beyond this period.

cso.rationale: Combined sewer discharges contain sewage and rainwater. EPA documents high bacteria levels in these discharges. We use a caution period of 72 hours after the reported end; the reported volume does not establish bacteria levels at a particular spot.
cso.source: U.S. EPA, Report to Congress on Impacts and Control of Combined Sewer Overflows and Sanitary Sewer Overflows (2004)

sso.rationale: Sanitary sewer discharges can contain concentrated sewage. We use a caution period of 72 hours after the reported end. Smaller reported volumes do not establish lower risk at a particular spot.
sso.source: U.S. EPA, Report to Congress on Impacts and Control of Combined Sewer Overflows and Sanitary Sewer Overflows (2004)

bypass.rationale: Wastewater can skip different treatment steps during a bypass. Reports do not always state which steps were skipped. We use a caution period of 72 hours after the reported end.
bypass.source: U.S. EPA, Report to Congress on Impacts and Control of Combined Sewer Overflows and Sanitary Sewer Overflows (2004)

plant_bypass.rationale: A treatment plant bypass skips one or more treatment steps. We use a caution period of 72 hours after the reported end.
plant_bypass.source: U.S. EPA, Report to Congress on Impacts and Control of Combined Sewer Overflows and Sanitary Sewer Overflows (2004)

blended.rationale: Blended discharges mix wastewater that skipped some treatment with treated wastewater. Treatment details vary. This rule uses 72 hours after the reported end.
blended.source: U.S. EPA, Report to Congress on Impacts and Control of Combined Sewer Overflows and Sanitary Sewer Overflows (2004)

beach_advisory.rationale: We use the authority's advisory status. DirtyWaterWatch does not decide when a beach reopens.

beach_closure.rationale: We use the authority's closure status. Read its notice for the location, dates and restrictions.

rain_advisory.rationale: We use the rainfall advisory and period stated by the issuing authority. The notice explains when its clock starts.
rain_advisory.source: Maine Healthy Beaches program; New York City DEP

hab_advisory.rationale: We list the authority's advisory and the date it was last confirmed. An old or missing update does not mean the advisory was lifted.
hab_advisory.source: Vermont Department of Health, Cyanobacteria Tracker; other issuing authorities

shellfish_closure.rationale: We use shellfish closure notices from the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management (DEM) and the Maine Department of Marine Resources (DMR). These restrict shellfish harvesting; they are not automatically swimming advisories.

annual_total.rationale: Monthly and yearly totals appear in history charts. They do not set a current status.

unknown.rationale: A notice we cannot fully read is shown with caution when it appears to report a discharge. Check the original notice for details.

lake.rationale: We use 96 hours after the reported discharge end for lakes. The cited research shows that bacteria can persist in still water and sediment. This is a site caution period, not a measured recovery time.
lake.source: Environment Agency (England), report SC250004/R (2026); Korajkic et al. (2019)

pond.rationale: We use 96 hours after the reported discharge end for ponds. Bacteria can persist in still water and sediment. This is a site caution period, not a measured recovery time.
pond.source: Environment Agency (England), report SC250004/R (2026); Korajkic et al. (2019)

reservoir.rationale: We use 96 hours after the reported discharge end for reservoirs. Bacteria can persist in still water and sediment. This is a site caution period, not a measured recovery time.
reservoir.source: Environment Agency (England), report SC250004/R (2026); Korajkic et al. (2019)

_example.rationale: Example of a water-specific window with its evidence; not enabled.

conditions.doc: Cold water and cloudy water can help bacteria persist. We show these conditions as context; they do not change the caution period. Flow can move and dilute a discharge, but does not establish water quality.
conditions.source: Kay et al. (2005); Korajkic et al. (2019); Jobson (1996)

yellow.default_source: Ackerman and Weisberg (2003); Arnold et al. (2017); Boehm et al. (2018); EU Bathing Water Directive, short-term pollution; N.H. RSA 485-A:8, III

principle: We err on the side of safety. When reports leave important details unclear, we show the uncertainty and explain the rule we use.

unresolved.doc: These records have no confirmed end time in the sources we track.
unresolved.ongoing_red_rationale: A report marked ongoing stays red until an end is found or 7 days pass. After 7 days we label the end unconfirmed rather than assume the discharge continues.
unresolved.unresolved_yellow_rationale: From day 7 to day 30, the map marks the end as unconfirmed. After day 30, the record remains flagged on its report and water pages.
unresolved.unknown_status_rationale: A discharge record with unclear status shows caution for 14 days after its report time. It then follows the rule for unconfirmed records.
unresolved.end_assumed_rationale: A report with no end is shown as unresolved for 30 days after it began; after that this site assumes the discharge ended and the record says the end was never reported.

source_outage._days_basis: build/status.py CONFIRM_DAYS (the existing 14-day age-out of a standing listing; common.UNREAD_GAP_DAYS and ingest/poll_periods.py GAP_DAYS match it); this value documents it and is not read
source_outage.rationale: An advisory the authority lists is shown as the authority's own for 14 days after the last read of the source that showed it. When a later read succeeds and no longer shows it, the advisory leaves the map after those 14 days. When the source could not be read at all since then, its end is not confirmed: the advisory stays on the map as end not confirmed, with the time of the last read that showed it, until the source can be read again. If that read lists it, it is shown as the authority's again from that read, and the unread time stays marked end not confirmed.
source_outage._decided: Owner, 2026-11-16: "disclosure is public safety", approving the recommendation that a standing advisory an authority listed must not turn grey just because the source could not be read (build/status.py outage_hold and carve_unread_gaps; common.no_ok_read_since and mark_unread_gaps).

implausible_end.rationale: An end time more than 31 days after we read a discharge report, or one before the discharge began, is most likely a typing error in the source. We do not draw a window from such an end: the report keeps the end as published, and the map treats the discharge as having no confirmed end. A planned window of some weeks keeps the end the authority gives, and so does an advisory.

sample_caution.rationale: Some agencies label a sample result a health risk but issue no advisory for it (Nebraska's Beach Watch marks E. coli above 235 per 100 mL as an elevated health risk; no advisory is issued for E. coli; Hawaii's Department of Health posts a notification, not an advisory, while it retests a beach whose routine sample was high; Texas Beach Watch's Medium level, enterococcus from 35 to 104 per 100 mL, at which the program recommends no advisory; a bloom reported to the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation for which it issued no advisory, confirmed or not yet assessed). The agency's words are quoted, and the site shows its own caution for 72 hours from the day of the sample, or until the agency closes its notice when that is later (Hawaii's retest notices stay posted until the retest is done; the Tennessee Department's end date for a bloom it followed up), never as the agency's advisory.
sample_caution.source: Nebraska Department of Water, Energy, and Environment, Beach Watch; Hawaii Department of Health, Clean Water Branch; Texas General Land Office, Texas Beach Watch; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation, HAB Advisory Status

day_start_caution.rationale: Some state lists give only the day a spill began, with no time of day and no end (Georgia's daily list of municipal sewage spills; the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality's table, which has given no end date since July 2024; the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation's Events Report, which gives no end date on most reports). These reports show caution for 72 hours from the start of that day, with the day shown as the precision; after that the end is marked unconfirmed until 30 days after the spill began.

reach.cap_rationale: We estimate downstream stretches to tidal water, the first lake or a maximum of 40 kilometres. A ring marks where the estimate stops. Contamination can travel beyond that point.
reach.source: U.S. Geological Survey, Network-Linked Data Index (NLDI) and the NHDPlus Version 2 river network; Jobson (1996), U.S. Geological Survey Water-Resources Investigations Report 96-4013

shoreline.doc: The Great Lakes and Lake St. Clair are shown like rivers, not coloured whole: a report from an outfall on one of these lakes colours a modeled stretch of shoreline at the outfall, and the lake's outline stays grey. The report still counts on the lake's page. Puget Sound is drawn the same way.

lakes.name: Lake St. Clair
lakes.rationale: Lake St. Clair joins Lake Huron to Lake Erie through the St. Clair and Detroit rivers and is part of the same Great Lakes system. It covers about 1,168 square kilometres and is shared with Ontario; a report from one outfall on its shore does not reach the whole lake, so the same shoreline stretch is drawn as on the Great Lakes.

lakes.name: Puget Sound
lakes.rationale: Puget Sound's main basin, off Seattle, covers about 470 square kilometres in the record used here, and the sound as a whole is several times larger. A report from one outfall on its shore does not reach the whole sound, so a stretch of shoreline is drawn at the outfall as on the Great Lakes: up to 20 kilometres along the shore each way, because tides and wind move the water along the shore in both directions. The stretch keeps the report's own advisory period, or this site's 72-hour caution after the reported end. The distance is our reading of the evidence from the Great Lakes and ocean shores, not a measurement in Puget Sound, and it may change. Contamination can reach beyond the stretch, and the rest of the sound is not shown as clean.

lakes.name: San Francisco Bay
lakes.rationale: San Francisco Bay is a tidal estuary of several hundred square kilometres (its map record alone covers about 606 square kilometres, and with San Pablo and Suisun bays the estuary is larger), shared by dozens of cities and sewer agencies. A report from one outfall on its shore does not reach the whole bay, so the report is shown along a stretch of the bay's shore at the outfall, up to 20 kilometres each way, as on the Great Lakes and the open ocean, and the bay's outline stays uncoloured. Tides carry water back and forth along the shore twice a day, so the stretch runs both ways. The distance is the one this site uses on the Great Lakes and the ocean shore; it has not been measured in this bay, and it may change. The stretch keeps the report's own advisory period, or our caution after the reported end. Contamination can reach beyond the stretch, and the rest of the bay is not shown as clean.

shoreline.rationale: On the Great Lakes a sewage report is shown along the shore at its outfall, not as a colour over the whole lake. We draw the shoreline up to 20 kilometres each way from the outfall. In the studies we found, sewage bacteria from very large overflows at Milwaukee fell to background levels 2 to 5 kilometres from the harbour; human sewage markers were found 8 kilometres offshore after severe overflows there; and models of the largest Chicago River overflows into Lake Michigan found plumes along the city's whole shore, whose beaches lie up to about 20 kilometres either side of the river mouth, lasting up to 24 days. Currents along a Great Lakes shore are driven by the wind and change direction every few days, so the stretch runs both ways. The distance is our reading of this evidence, toward the longer end because viruses outlast the bacteria that are measured; it is not a measurement at any outfall, and it may change. The stretch keeps the report's own advisory period, or our 96-hour lake caution after the reported end. Contamination can reach beyond the stretch, and the rest of the lake is not shown as clean.
shoreline.source: Distance: McLellan and Jensen Hollis, Bacteria Source, Transport and Fate Study, Phase 1, Volume 3 (Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District; University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee Great Lakes WATER Institute contribution 470), the May 2004 overflows; McLellan et al. (2007), Journal of Great Lakes Research 33(3): 566; Newton et al. (2013), Microbial Ecology 65; Weiskerger (2022), Michigan State University dissertation, doi:10.25335/gbpd-ac22; viruses outlasting indicator bacteria: Boehm et al. (2018); direction: NOAA Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory, EEGLE nearshore current observations in southern Lake Michigan (alongshore currents driven by the wind, with 3 to 5 day reversals). Duration: the report's advisory period, or the 96-hour lake caution (Environment Agency (England), report SC250004/R (2026); Korajkic et al. (2019)). Shoreline: the lake's outline where it meets land in the U.S. Census Bureau's 2023 cartographic state outlines (cb_2023_us_state_500k); for a lake record with no outline of its own, the state's waters in the lake from the Census Bureau's TIGER/Line 2023 state boundaries (tl_2023_us_state) less that land.
shoreline.ocean_rationale: A sewage report on the open ocean (the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean, or the Gulf of America, the Gulf of Mexico) is shown along the shore at its outfall or reported location, never as a colour over the ocean. We draw the state's ocean shore up to 20 kilometres each way from that point. The stretch follows the open coast across inlets and passes narrower than about 2 kilometres, rather than into the lagoons and bays behind them; where a bay or sound opens more widely to the sea, the stretch follows its shore too, and the report is also shown on that water. In the studies we found, waves and wind carried untreated wastewater along ocean beaches near San Diego for up to about 20 kilometres, and modelled plumes reached beaches about 25 kilometres from their source, at speeds of about 8 to 14 kilometres a day; the direction follows the waves and wind and changes with them, so the stretch runs both ways. Our Great Lakes shoreline distance is the same, 20 kilometres each way. The distance is our reading of this evidence, not a measurement at any outfall, and it may change. The stretch keeps the report's own advisory period, or our caution after the reported end. Contamination can reach beyond the stretch and offshore, and the rest of the coast is not shown as clean.
shoreline.ocean_source: Distance and direction: Feddersen, Boehm, Giddings, Wu and Liden (2021), Modeling untreated wastewater evolution and swimmer illness for four wastewater infrastructure scenarios in the San Diego-Tijuana (US/MX) border region, GeoHealth 5, e2021GH000490 (wave-driven surfzone currents carrying wastewater up to about 20 km alongshore, citing Zimmer-Faust et al. 2021; modelled plumes reaching beaches about 25 km north of the source; alongshore transport of about 8 to 14 km a day, and of about 10 km a day in surfzone tracer studies, Grant et al. 2005 and Grimes et al. 2020); viruses outlasting indicator bacteria: Boehm et al. (2018). Shore: the state's waters from the U.S. Census Bureau's TIGER/Line 2023 state boundaries (tl_2023_us_state), which run to the state's offshore line, less the land of its 2023 cartographic state outlines (cb_2023_us_state_500k).
shoreline._internal_doc: build/shoreline.py. A lake record is a shoreline lake when its wikidata or gnis_id is listed, or its name is listed and its area is at least name_min_area_km2 (a 0.7 km2 New York pond is also named Lake Superior), or (min_area_km2 set) any lake or reservoir at least that large. min_area_km2 is null: the other lakes over 1,000 km2 in the records (Lake Champlain VT and NY, live, 1,181 km2; Lake Okeechobee FL, 1,229 km2; Pamlico Sound NC, recorded as a lake, 4,083 km2) keep today's whole-water behaviour until that is decided. each_way_km 20 (code review of 2026-11-04; first built with 40, the river cap applied both ways): fecal indicators at background 2 to 5 km from the Milwaukee breakwall after the 4.5-billion-gallon May 2004 overflows (MMSD BSTF Phase 1 vol. 3, sec. 4.3.3; fecal coliform 90% gone in 6 to 8 h in the lake, Zanoni 1978 as cited there), human Bacteroides and Lachnospiraceae markers at least 8 km offshore after severe overflows (Newton 2013), the Chicago backflow plumes 7.9 to 291 km2 persisting up to 24 days with every Chicago Park District beach (about 15 km north and 20 km south of the river mouth) susceptible (Weiskerger 2022); GLERL EEGLE alongshore currents of about 6 to 16 cm/s (about 5 to 14 km a day) reversing on 3 to 5 day scales.
